turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good morning, please come in and have a seat. What brings you along today?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. Thank you for fitting me in. I have come chiefly for a short note for the walking club at the community centre, and, if I may, my right knee has been rather stiff.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of course, we can sort both. Tell me a bit about that knee, how has it been for you?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It is the right one, Doctor. It is a stiffness more than a pain. It began last winter, or it may have been the winter before that, and I cannot date it properly, I am afraid.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's all right, we don't need the exact week. When do you notice it most?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): In the mornings, after I have been sitting with the newspaper. Once I have walked as far as the gate it eases. It is a nuisance, not something severe.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling, or does the knee give way under you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling that I have noticed, and it has never given way. I am quite steady on it.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you been using for it?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Only Panado, Doctor. Two of the five hundred milligram tablets when it plays up, perhaps two or three times in a week, not every day.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): So a gram of Panado by mouth, as you need it. Anything else, a rub or something on prescription?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor, nothing else. I did not wish to begin a stronger tablet without your advice.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sensible. Now, the sister took your pressure in the passage and she was worried. She has written one hundred and seventy-two over one hundred and four.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): That does sound high. I must say I believe it is the white coat, Doctor. At the Clicks pharmacy last month the assistant said the reading was perfectly ordinary.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): It may be. Let me ask a little, and then I will check it myself. Any headaches lately?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor, no headaches.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, or a tight feeling when you walk?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): None at all. I walked from the parking without the slightest trouble.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): And dizziness, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, neither of those.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. We will sit quietly a second. Right, on my cuff I am getting one hundred and fifty-six over ninety-four, and your pulse is seventy-six, nice and regular.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Still higher than I would like, though kinder than the sister's figure. I do become rather tense in a doctor's rooms. It has always been the case.

[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): I hear you. Turning it over, it could be white-coat, it could be that the cuff was a little snug outside, or the pressure could genuinely be sitting up. I am not going to decide which of those it is just yet.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand, and I would prefer not to be labelled in haste.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you taking anything for blood pressure at the moment?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): There is the water tablet. I swallow it in the morning with my tea. A doctor in Pietermaritzburg started it, and I think the dose is twelve and a half milligrams, though I would not swear to that.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): You do not have the proper name, off a box at home?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I am sorry, Doctor. I cannot tell you the name. The label has worn quite away, and it is simply the water tablet to me.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): And is that every morning, as it was prescribed?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I am meant to take it every morning. In honesty I miss it some days, perhaps twice in a week, when I am rushing for the train.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): When was it started, even roughly?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Around the time of my sister's gathering in Durban, or just after, and I cannot put a year to it. My father had a stroke, incidentally, a long while back. He smoked a great deal. I myself have never smoked.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am glad you mentioned that, and we will keep your father's stroke in mind. You still manage your walking, seeing as you want the club note?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. Three mornings a week, on the flat, at a gentle pace. That is all.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): That is a solid habit. Did you battle on the road this morning? I heard the N1 was a proper mess.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Indeed I did. I sat at the William Nicol robot for an age. I left home at half past six and I was late for the errand before this.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame. And the weather cannot make up its mind, cold at dawn and warm by tea time.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Quite so. My granddaughter says the jacarandas are confused this year. She is in grade four, and there is a recorder concert on Friday, heaven help the parents.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Recorders. I still carry the scars from my own child's recorder year. Is she nervous about it?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): She is remarkably composed. She has a solo of about eight bars. We are far more nervous than she is. My wife has ironed the uniform twice already.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the whole family pitching up?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): The cousins from Benoni are driving through, if the bakkie behaves. My brother-in-law swears by that old Hilux. It has attended more braais than I have.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): A Hilux will outlast the lot of us. Did you see any of the cricket, or were you on grandparent duty?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I saw the last hour. The Proteas were rather untidy in the field, though the batting was fine. I do prefer a Test to the short form.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am the same. Five days, if one can get them. The Wanderers sounded loud on the radio.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): My neighbour had the braai going and the radio on the veranda. I declined a second chop. One must pretend at discipline now and then.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha. Wise enough. Let me come back to the medical side.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, of course, Doctor.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): I have had a proper look at the right knee. There is no swelling, it is not warm, and it bends fully. I cannot find anything there that worries me.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): That is most reassuring. Thank you, Doctor.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, and I mean this as possibilities rather than a label, this may be white-coat hypertension, or your pressure may be truly raised. Both stay open. I will not call it hypertension today.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I appreciate that caution, Doctor.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am not starting any new tablets today. We will leave the water tablet exactly as it is, missed doses and all, until we have a proper run of readings.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): I am grateful. I had rather hoped you would not add another tablet this morning.

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): What I would like you to do is to get a validated home monitor, Clicks can show you one, and check the pressure each morning and each evening for two weeks. Write every single reading down.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Morning and evening, for two weeks. I shall buy the machine on the way home.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. If those home readings are still high, then we will arrange bloods, kidney function and a cholesterol. Not today, only if they stay up.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Only if they remain high. I understand.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): And I will see you here in two weeks with that notebook, whatever the numbers say. Ask reception to book it as you leave.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. I shall be here. May I still have the note for the walking club?

[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. I will write a short note that the knee is fit for ordinary walking with the club. If you get chest pain, or a sudden severe headache, do not wait for me, go straight to casualty. Enjoy the recorders on Friday.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall do exactly that. You have been most kind, Doctor. Thank you.

spec.situation: Patient attends for something minor (a knee or a form) and the nurse finds high BP; BP read aloud twice with different numbers; patient says it is white coat; family history of stroke said in passing; no tablets started today, home monitoring arranged.
features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

bad.reason: Current oral water tablet for blood pressure supported; dose is uncertain and actual use misses about twice weekly.
bad.text: water tablet (dose=12.5 mg, route=oral, frequency=every morning, indication=blood pressure, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Heart rate was described as 'nice and regular' (regular pulse rhythm), not just 76 bpm.
The water tablet dose/frequency was recorded as every morning, but the patient said they miss it some days, about twice a week, when rushing for the train; current use is not consistently daily.
The patient reported a normal blood pressure reading at Clicks pharmacy last month ('perfectly ordinary'), relevant to the possible white-coat hypertension assessment.
The doctor advised follow-up in two weeks with the home blood pressure notebook 'whatever the numbers say' and to book at reception on leaving.
